name: cpgf callback (GCallback / GCallbackList)
baseline: Boost.Signals2 1.46.0 and libsigc++ 2.2.8 (signal/slot and callback invocation)
workload: Invoking a callback bound to an inline member, non-inline member, virtual member, global function or functor taking one int (100M calls), and emitting a signal with 0, 5, 10 and 50 connected slots (10M emissions), timed with clock() on Windows XP.
claimed_speedup: Single-slot calls (VC 9): inline member 781 ms vs Boost.Signals2 3547 ms (4.5x, derived from page data) and libsigc++ 766 ms (parity); global function 719 vs 3578 ms (5.0x, derived); functor 468 vs 3156 ms (6.7x, derived). GCC 4.5.2: inline member 1047 vs 1875 ms (1.8x, derived), functor 515 vs 1547 ms (3.0x, derived), libsigc++ about equal (1000 and 516 ms). Signal emission (VC 9): 5 slots 641 ms vs libsigc++ 2734 ms (4.3x, derived) and Boost.Signals2 8797 ms (13.7x, derived); 10 slots 1109 vs 3328 ms (3.0x vs libsigc++) and 15203 ms; 50 slots 6735 vs 7875 ms (1.17x vs libsigc++) and 64813 ms (9.6x vs Boost). GCC 5 slots: 578 vs 2547 ms (libsigc++) vs 7515 ms (Boost).
compiler_and_flags: VC 9 (Visual Studio 2008 Express) with -O2, _SECURE_SCL=0, _HAS_ITERATOR_DEBUGGING=0; MinGW GCC 4.5.2 with -O3. Harness source: test/benchmark/callback/benchmarkcallback.cpp in the repo.
hardware: Intel Pentium Dual CPU E2180 2GHz, 4G RAM, Windows XP SP2
tradeoffs: Part of the larger cpgf library (reflection, serialization, Lua/V8/Python/SpiderMonkey binding, callback, tweening); the callback headers (gcallback.h, gcallbacklist.h) are the relevant piece. C++03 code base, requires C++ exceptions and RTTI per the README. The author states the project is not continued and points to eventpp for the callback list feature.
caveats: The numbers date from about 2011 (Pentium E2180, Windows XP, VC 9, GCC 4.5.2, Boost 1.46.0, libsigc++ 2.2.8) and the page itself says new hardware will produce quite different results; newer Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++ releases were not measured. Single run per cell timed with clock(), no repeat or variance reported. The Boost column is the default thread-safe boost::signals2::signal type in the harness. Single-slot cpgf calls are roughly on par with libsigc++ (781 vs 766 ms VC 9; 1047 vs 1000 ms GCC) and 10 to 22 times slower than a native call the compiler can inline (46-47 ms); the page notes FastDelegate code from CodeProject was about twice as fast as cpgf callback but is excluded from the table. No comparison against std::function or std::signal-like facilities. The benchmark is for the callback component, not for the reflection or serialization parts the seed list described; filed under the stdlib-replacements category that holds std::function (same placement as larspensjo/simplesignal), the orchestrator may re-file it. Source of the benchmark was read but not built or rerun.

name: Enchantum
baseline: magic_enum (compile-time enum reflection to string); simple_enum and conjure_enum also compared
workload: Generated translation units (benchmarks/gen.py) declaring 32 to 200 enum class types with 16 to 200 members each and calling to_string once per enum through a volatile; compile time averaged over 10 runs, plus object and executable size on Clang.
claimed_speedup: README compile-time table, GCC: Small (200 enums, range -128..128) enchantum 6.0 s vs magic_enum 47 s (7.8x, derived from page data); Big 2.7 vs 21 s (7.8x, derived); Ideal Range 3 vs 8.1 s (2.7x, derived); Large Range 15.9 s vs magic_enum timeout (over 20 minutes). Default out-of-bounds checking (numbers in parentheses): Small 8.2 vs 47 s (5.7x, derived), Big 3.3 vs 21 s (6.4x, derived). Clang Small 5.8 vs 47 s; MSVC Small 15.8 (37.4) vs 80 s. Clang object size Small 275 KB vs magic_enum 732 KB (2.7x, derived), Big 84 vs 1307 KB (15.6x, derived); executable Small 40 vs 95 KB. Author's own project full rebuild 2 min to 1 min 26 s after switching from magic_enum.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.0 and Clang 20.1.2 with -O3, MSVC 19.44 (VS 2022) with /Ox; 10 runs averaged; exact command lines not stated. Test files generated by benchmarks/gen.py (magic_enum range set via MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE_MIN/MAX, enchantum via ENCHANTUM_MIN_RANGE/MAX_RANGE, conjure_enum with FIX8_CONJURE_ENUM_MINIMAL).
hardware: Windows 10 machine, CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: C++17 header-only enum reflection without macros; reflects values inside a configurable range (ENCHANTUM_MIN_RANGE/MAX_RANGE) like magic_enum; README lists no support for wide strings and points to docs/limitations.md. The default setting adds an out-of-bounds check (ENCHANTUM_CHECK_OUT_OF_BOUNDS_BY=2) that detects enums not fully reflected, at extra compile time.
caveats: First-party benchmark; CPU model missing, so it falls short of tier A, although the generator (benchmarks/gen.py) is public and its test-case parameters match the README table. The bold headline numbers appear to be with the out-of-bounds check disabled; the README says the parenthesised values are with the default setting (about 1.2x to 2.1x slower on GCC, and MSVC Small 37.4 vs 15.8 s), so the default-configuration win over magic_enum is smaller (for example 5.7x rather than 7.8x on GCC Small). simple_enum is faster on the Ideal Range case (2.7 vs 3 s on GCC); magic_enum is given the same ranges as enchantum (up to -1024..1024, where it timed out), and the Ideal Range case (0..50), where magic_enum is only 2.7x slower, is the least range-inflated comparison. No comparison with a hand-written switch or std::string_view table, and no runtime lookup benchmark. The Reddit post by a friend of the author linked from the README (cost of enum to string, C++26 reflection vs the old ways) was not reachable; no independent reproduction found.
